title: Turbofans and turboprops compared
examples: What is the difference between a turbofan and a turboprop?
Why do some planes still have propellers?
What is bypass air in a jet engine?

figure.name: x-compare

left.title: Turbofan
points: Big ducted fan at the front

figure.verdict: Long fast trips: turbofan. Short hops: turboprop

explain.say: Turbofans and turboprops both have a jet engine core: a compressor, a combustion chamber and a turbine. The difference is what that core spins: a big fan inside a duct, or a propeller out in the open.

draw.name: x-compare

left.title: Turbofan
points: Big ducted fan at the front

draw.verdict: Long fast trips: turbofan. Short hops: turboprop

explain.say: In a turbofan, most of the air from the front fan bypasses the core and flows around it. On the newest airliners about ten times more air goes around the core than through it, and this bypass air makes most of the thrust.

draw.name: x-compare

left.title: Turbofan
points: Big ducted fan at the front

draw.verdict: Long fast trips: turbofan. Short hops: turboprop

explain.say: In a turboprop, the turbine drives a propeller through a gearbox, because a propeller must turn much more slowly than a turbine. A propeller moves a lot of air gently, which saves fuel at lower speeds.

draw.name: x-compare

left.title: Turbofan
points: Big ducted fan at the front

draw.verdict: Long fast trips: turbofan. Short hops: turboprop

explain.say: Propeller tips lose efficiency as they near the speed of sound, so turboprops cruise slower, around 500 to 650 kilometres per hour. Turbofans keep their fan inside a duct and cruise at about 850.

faq.a: Bypass air is air that the front fan pushes around the engine core instead of through it. Moving lots of air gently is more efficient and quieter than blasting a little air very fast, so bypass air makes most of a modern turbofan's thrust.

faq.q: Why do some planes still use propellers?
faq.a: On short routes at lower speeds, a turboprop burns noticeably less fuel than a jet and can use shorter runways, so regional airlines use them for hops between smaller airports.
asks: Why do small airliners have propellers?

faq.q: Why can't turboprops fly as fast as jets?
faq.a: Propeller tips spin round while also moving forward, so they reach the speed of sound before the plane does. Shock waves then waste energy, so turboprops usually cruise below about 650 kilometres per hour.

faq.q: Is a turboprop a jet engine?
faq.a: Its core is a gas turbine, the same kind of engine as a jet, but almost all its power goes into turning the propeller instead of making a hot jet. So it is a jet engine that drives a propeller.
asks: Does a turboprop have a jet engine inside?

faq.q: Why does a turboprop need a gearbox?
faq.a: The turbine spins many thousands of times a minute, but a propeller works best far slower, roughly 1,000 to 2,000 turns a minute. A reduction gearbox slows the spin and increases the turning force.
asks: How fast does a propeller spin?

facts: The newest airliner turbofans have bypass ratios of about 10 to 12, sending that many times more air around the core than through it.
The ATR 72 and the De Havilland Dash 8 are common turboprop airliners on short regional routes.

quiz.say: A regional airline flies short hops of about 300 kilometres between small towns. Which engine is likely to save the most fuel?
quiz.show: Best engine for short, slower hops?
quiz.why: On short, slower routes a propeller moves lots of air gently, which is the most fuel-efficient way to make thrust.

wrong.1: A pure turbojet blasts a small amount of air very fast and is the thirstiest kind of jet.
wrong.2: A rocket carries its own oxygen and burns fuel extremely quickly; airliners never use them.
